subject: Egyptian vulture
title: A Vulture Picks Up Rocks and Throws Them. Nobody Has to Teach It

scenes.text: A vulture found a meal it couldn't bite open. So it picked up a rock.
An ostrich egg is too big and too tough for an Egyptian vulture's beak. Pecking gets it nowhere.
So the bird searches the ground, sometimes fifty yards away, for a stone it can carry.
It stands tall, lifts its head, and whips the stone down at the shell. About half its throws hit.
Jane Goodall reported it from Tanzania in 1966, in the journal Nature.
The strangest part came later. Chicks raised without any adults threw stones anyway. It's built in.

description:
The Egyptian vulture cracks ostrich eggs by throwing stones at them.
The behaviour was described by Jane van Lawick-Goodall and Hugo van Lawick in Nature in 1966, after they watched vultures in Tanzania pick up stones in their beaks, raise their heads and whip the stones down at ostrich eggs until the shells broke; in follow-up tests the birds did the same with eggs the researchers set out. The vultures search up to about 50 yards for a suitable stone and hit the egg with roughly 40 to 60 percent of their throws. Later work with young birds reared away from adults (Thouless and colleagues, 1989) found that stone-throwing appears without any teaching; what the birds have to learn is that an ostrich egg is food, which happens once they taste a cracked one.
Which other animal tool-user surprised you most? Comment below.
first_comment: The birds prefer rounded, egg-shaped stones, a hint that the habit began with throwing eggs. Which animal tool-user surprised you most?
